contexts.title: ECON 110 week 6 handout: price elasticity of demand
contexts.text:
ECON 110 - PRINCIPLES OF MICROECONOMICS
Week 6 handout: price elasticity of demand. Prof. R. Ansbach, Fall 2026.

Course admin (reminder)
- Grade weights: problem sets 30%, midterm 30%, final exam 40%. Your problem-set score is the average of your best 8 of 10 sets.
- Final exam: Thursday 10 December, 9:00-12:00, Hollingworth Hall. A formula sheet is provided.
- Office hours move to Tuesday 2-4 pm this week only.

1. Definition
Price elasticity of demand (PED) measures how strongly quantity demanded responds to a change in price:
PED = (% change in quantity demanded) / (% change in price).
PED is negative for normal demand curves; we usually talk about its absolute value.
- |PED| > 1: elastic (quantity responds more than proportionally)
- |PED| = 1: unit elastic
- |PED| < 1: inelastic

2. Why we use the midpoint (arc) method
Simple percentage changes depend on the direction you measure in: going from 10 to 12 is +20%, but going back from 12 to 10 is -16.7%. The midpoint method divides each change by the AVERAGE of the start and end values, so the answer is the same in both directions:
% change in Q = (Q2 - Q1) / ((Q1 + Q2) / 2)
% change in P = (P2 - P1) / ((P1 + P2) / 2)
Use the midpoint method on problem sets and exams unless a question says otherwise.

3. Worked example
Coffee kiosk: price rises from $3.00 to $3.50, cups sold per day fall from 400 to 360.
% change in Q = -40 / 380 = -10.5%
% change in P = 0.50 / 3.25 = 15.4%
PED = -0.68, so demand is inelastic. Revenue rises from $1,200 to $1,260.

4. Estimates from the readings (Aldmere Transit Study; fictional data for class use)
- City bus ridership, short run (first year after a fare change): -0.3
- City bus ridership, long run (after five years): -0.7
- Cinema tickets: -1.6
- Cigarettes: -0.4
Long-run demand is more elastic because people have time to find substitutes (move closer to work, buy a bike, car-pool).

5. Elasticity and total revenue
If demand is elastic, a price increase reduces total revenue; if it is inelastic, a price increase raises total revenue.

6. Common mistakes
Mixing up percentage points and percent; forgetting the negative sign; using simple percentage changes when the midpoint method is asked for.
contexts.notes: SQLEC-001: midpoint: dQ = -300 / 1,050 = -28.57%; dP = 10 / 45 = 22.22%; PED = -1.29, elastic (revenue 48,000 -> 45,000). Trap: simple percentages give -25% / +25% = -1.0, 'unit elastic'. SQLEC-002: weights 30/30/40: 0.3 x 91 + 0.3 x 72 = 48.9; (80 - 48.9) / 0.4 = 77.75. Trap: equal weights give 77; 'best 8 of 10' is noise because the student states the average. SQLEC-003 (lookup): long-run bus ridership -0.7; the short-run -0.3 is the neighbouring-row trap.
